h: Dripping chips and a newer, post-war corner
p: The Black Country Living Museum isn't standing still. A big development has been adding a whole new area that carries the story forward into the 1940s, 50s and 60s, with buildings from that era rescued from around the region. It means grandparents get to point at the shops and homes of their childhood while the kids explore the older Victorian streets, which makes for a lot of chatter on the walk round.

Don't leave without visiting the fish and chip shop. Hobbs and Sons fries in beef dripping the traditional way, and it's become one of the most talked-about bits of the whole museum. The queue can stretch at lunchtime, so it pays to eat a little early. The old sweet shop and the pub are other favourites, and the traditional schoolroom, where a strict teacher may well put you through your paces, is great fun for school-age children.

Pace yourself. With mines, canal trips, the fairground and dozens of buildings, there's more here than most people manage in one visit. Pick a few must-dos, check the day's demonstration timings when you arrive and build the rest around them.

Just up the road, the Wren's Nest National Nature Reserve is famous for its fossils, including the trilobite known locally as the Dudley Bug, and it's a cracking spot for a bit of fresh air after a day of history. Dudley Zoo and Castle is neighbouring too, and Birmingham's city centre is close enough for an evening out if you're stopping over.
